title: Impact of Pharmaceutical Patent Approval on Company Returns

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy  
Causal method: Short-horizon event study.  
Why: Patent approval is a sharply-timed, firm–specific information shock. When financial markets are semi-strong-form efficient, the causal impact of the news on equity value is revealed almost instantaneously in abnormal stock returns around the announcement.  
Key assumptions  
• Market efficiency: prices incorporate new public information immediately, so abnormal returns outside the short event window are zero in expectation.  
• No confounding events: no other firm-specific news overlaps the chosen window (verified with ±1 / ±3 robustness windows).  
• Correct model of normal returns: the market-model abnormal return ARit = rit − βi·rmt is mean-zero in the absence of the event (βi is given in the data, so is estimated out-of-sample).  

## 2. R Code
```r
###############################################################
# Impact of pharmaceutical patent approval on stock returns
###############################################################
library(data.table)
library(lmtest)
library(sandwich)

# 1. Read data -------------------------------------------------
path <- "experiments/exp_b/data/s61_data.csv"
dt <- fread(path)

# 2. Compute abnormal return (market model) --------------------
# AR_it = r_it - beta_i * r_mt
dt[, AR := ret - beta * mkt_ret]

# 3. Cumulative abnormal return (CAR) --------------------------
# Main window  : [-1, +1]
# Robustness 1 : [-3, +3]
# Robustness 2 : [-5, +5]  (only if days exist)
windows <- list(w1 = c(-1,1),
                w3 = c(-3,3),
                w5 = c(-5,5))

get_CAR <- function(d, win){
  d[event_day %between% win, .(CAR = sum(AR)), by = stock_id]
}

car_list <- lapply(windows, function(w) get_CAR(dt, w))
names(car_list) <- names(windows)

# 4. Average CARs & t-tests -----------------------------------
car_stats <- lapply(car_list, function(df){
  t_out <- t.test(df$CAR)
  list(mean = mean(df$CAR),
       t    = as.numeric(t_out$statistic),
       p    = as.numeric(t_out$p.value))
})

print("Average CARs (mean, t-stat, p-value):")
print(car_stats)

# 5. Regression-based robustness -------------------------------
# Panel regression with firm fixed effects and clustered s.e.
# Treat the event window [0,+1] as “treatment”.
dt[, treat := (event_day >= 0 & event_day <= 1)]

reg <- lm(ret ~ mkt_ret + treat, data = dt)
se_clust <- vcovCL(reg, cluster = dt$stock_id)
cat("\nRegression result (treat coefficient):\n")
print(coeftest(reg, vcov = se_clust)["treat", ])

# 6. Additional check: placebo window (-10,-6) -----------------
dt[, placebo := (event_day >= -10 & event_day <= -6)]
reg_placebo <- lm(ret ~ mkt_ret + placebo, data = dt)
se_clust2 <- vcovCL(reg_placebo, cluster = dt$stock_id)
cat("\nPlacebo result (should be ≈0):\n")
print(coeftest(reg_placebo, vcov = se_clust2)["placebo", ])
```

The script:  
1. Reads the CSV.  
2. Calculates abnormal returns using each firm’s provided β.  
3. Builds CARs for three windows.  
4. Prints the mean CAR, t-statistic and p-value.  
5. Runs a panel regression (firm clustered s.e.) with an event dummy.  
6. Performs a placebo test in a pre-event window to confirm no spurious effect.

## 3. Expected Findings  
Economic intuition and prior literature on drug approvals suggest a positive surprise: successful patents increase future monopoly rents, so investors should bid up the stock.  
• Sign: Positive.  
• Magnitude: For a narrow [-1,+1] window, an average CAR of roughly +1.5 % to +3 % is plausible. Wider windows should show a slightly larger but still single-digit CAR.  
• The regression “treat” coefficient should be positive and significant (t-stat > 2), while the placebo coefficient should be close to zero and insignificant.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Compare stock returns before and after patent approval.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Patent approvals lead to a significant increase in drug-company CAR.
